# Visualization {#sec-visualization}

The `gstudio` package returns analysis results as standard `data.frame` objects, which plug directly into ggplot2. This chapter shows the recommended plotting patterns for allele frequency data, population maps, and population graphs.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library( gstudio )
library( dplyr )
library( ggplot2 )
library( ggraph )
data( arapat )
```

## Allele Frequency Plots

`frequencies()` returns a tidy data frame with columns `Locus`, `Allele`, and `Frequency` (plus `Stratum` when partitioned). Pass it directly to `geom_bar()`.

### Single locus

```{r}
arapat |>
  frequencies( loci = "LTRS" ) |>
  ggplot( aes( x = Allele, y = Frequency ) ) +
  geom_bar( stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue" ) +
  labs( title = "Allele Frequencies at LTRS" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Partitioned by stratum

When `stratum` is supplied, `frequencies()` zero-fills missing allele/stratum combinations so dodged and faceted plots are correctly aligned. Filter with `Frequency > 0` beforehand if you prefer to show only observed alleles.

```{r}
freqs <- arapat |>
  frequencies( loci = "LTRS", stratum = "Species" )

freqs |>
  ggplot( aes( x = Allele, y = Frequency, fill = Stratum ) ) +
  geom_bar( stat = "identity", position = "dodge" ) +
  labs( title = "LTRS Allele Frequencies by Species" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Faceted across strata

Here the zero-filled alleles are dropped with `filter()` before plotting:

```{r}
freqs |>
  filter( Frequency > 0 ) |>
  ggplot( aes( x = Allele, y = Frequency, fill = Allele ) ) +
  geom_bar( stat = "identity" ) +
  facet_wrap( ~Stratum ) +
  labs( title = "LTRS Frequencies by Species" ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme( legend.position = "none" )
```

## Spatial Sampling Maps

`strata_coordinates()` aggregates individual records to population centroids, returning a data frame with `Stratum`, `Longitude`, and `Latitude` columns ready for `geom_point()`.  Points alone, however, say little about *where* the samples are.  A light outline of the land behind them gives that context.

### A Base Map

The [Natural Earth](https://www.naturalearthdata.com) boundaries in the `rnaturalearth` package (with its data package `rnaturalearthdata`; install both once with `install.packages()`) are returned as `sf` objects, which `geom_sf()` draws directly.  The base map below has a grey land outline, labels for the two seas, and a simple north arrow drawn with `annotate()`; `coord_sf()` sets the extent.  It is an ordinary ggplot, so it can be stored and reused for every map of the region.

```{r}
#| message: false
countries <- c( "Mexico", "United States of America" )
land      <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries( country = countries,
                                          scale = "medium",
                                          returnclass = "sf" )

baja_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf( data = land,
           fill = "grey92",
           colour = "grey55",
           linewidth = 0.3 ) +
  annotate( "text",
            x = -111.3,
            y = 27.6,
            label = "Sea of Cortez",
            angle = -52,
            colour = "steelblue4",
            fontface = "italic",
            size = 3.2 ) +
  annotate( "text",
            x = -116.0,
            y = 25.0,
            label = "Pacific Ocean",
            colour = "steelblue4",
            fontface = "italic",
            size = 3.5 ) +
  annotate( "segment",
            x = -109.0,
            xend = -109.0,
            y = 31.0,
            yend = 32.0,
            arrow = arrow( length = unit( 2.5, "mm" ),
                           type = "closed" ) ) +
  annotate( "text",
            x = -109.0,
            y = 32.3,
            label = "N",
            fontface = "bold" ) +
  coord_sf( xlim = c( -117.5, -108.5 ),
            ylim = c( 22.5, 32.5 ),
            expand = FALSE ) +
  labs( x = NULL, y = NULL ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme( panel.background = element_rect( fill = "aliceblue",
                                          colour = NA ) )
```

Because geographic coordinates are longitude and latitude, the sample data can be added as ordinary layers; layers added later are drawn on top, so the points sit above the land.  The north arrow points up the page, which is true north here because `coord_sf()` draws unprojected longitude and latitude.  For a projected map, or a scale bar, the `ggspatial` package's `annotation_north_arrow()` and `annotation_scale()` do the same job.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 6
coords <- arapat |>
  strata_coordinates()

baja_map +
  geom_point( aes( x = Longitude, y = Latitude ),
              data = coords,
              size = 2.5,
              shape = 21,
              fill = "steelblue" ) +
  labs( title = "Araptus attenuatus Sampling Locations" )
```

Individual-level data works just as well when you want within-population spread:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
baja_map +
  geom_point( aes( x = Longitude, y = Latitude, fill = Species ),
              data = arapat,
              size = 2,
              shape = 21,
              alpha = 0.7 )
```

## Population Graph Visualization

For a quick look, `plot()` on a Population Graph returns a ggplot (nodes sized by their `size` attribute — within-population genetic variability for graphs from `popgraph()` — or by degree when there is none, and filled by a `Region` attribute when present; geographic coordinates used when the graph carries them, arrows for directed graphs); see the Population Graphs article for its options. For fully custom figures, use the [ggraph](https://ggraph.data-imaginist.com) package, which extends ggplot2 for graph objects and works natively with `popgraph`/`igraph` objects. Install it once with `install.packages("ggraph")`.

### Force-Directed Layout

Build a population graph from the `arapat` dataset and plot it with a Fruchterman-Reingold layout. Node and edge aesthetics map directly to vertex and edge attributes.

```{r}
graph <- arapat |>
  population_graph( stratum = "Species" )

igraph::V( graph )$degree <- igraph::degree( graph )

graph |>
  ggraph( layout = "fr" ) +
  geom_edge_link( color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5 ) +
  geom_node_point( aes( fill = degree ), size = 5, shape = 21 ) +
  geom_node_label( aes( label = name ), repel = TRUE, size = 2.5 ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_graph() +
  labs( title = "Araptus attenuatus Population Graph" )
```

### On a Map with `plot()`

`plot()` draws a Population Graph on another ggplot when it is given as `base =`: the graph's edges and nodes go on top, and the base map's coordinate system and extent are kept.  A graph decorated with coordinates (`decorate_graph()`) is placed geographically:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
data( lopho )
data( baja )

lopho_dec <- lopho |>
  decorate_graph( baja, stratum = "Population" )

lopho_dec |>
  plot( base = baja_map )
```

The same `base =` works for a gravity field (@sec-genetic-gravity), whose source-sink surface is drawn between the map and the graph.  @sec-gravity-map crops that surface to land and draws it with and without the graph on top.

### Geographic Layout with ggraph

With ggraph, use `layout = "manual"` with longitude and latitude pulled from vertex attributes set by `decorate_graph()`.  A ggraph plot starts with no layers, so adding `geom_sf()` first puts the land underneath the edges and nodes, and `coord_sf()` keeps geographic proportions.

Use `scale_edge_width(range = c(min, max))` to control the rendered line width in mm. Dividing weights inside `aes()` has no effect because ggraph's default scale auto-normalises to the data range regardless — the scale absorbs any constant factor. For non-linear transforms (log, normalize), add a pre-computed edge attribute with `igraph::E(graph)$attr <- ...` before plotting.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
lopho_dec |>
  ggraph( layout = "manual",
          x = igraph::V( lopho_dec )$Longitude,
          y = igraph::V( lopho_dec )$Latitude ) +
  geom_sf( data = land,
           fill = "grey92",
           colour = "grey55",
           linewidth = 0.3 ) +
  geom_edge_link( aes( width = weight ),
                  color = "grey40",
                  show.legend = FALSE ) +
  scale_edge_width( range = c( 0.3, 2.5 ), guide = "none" ) +
  geom_node_point( aes( size = size, color = Region ),
                   show.legend = FALSE ) +
  geom_node_label( aes( label = name ), repel = TRUE, size = 2.5 ) +
  coord_sf( xlim = c( -116, -108.5 ),
            ylim = c( 22.5, 32.5 ) ) +
  labs( title = "Lophocereus Population Graph",
        x = NULL,
        y = NULL ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Directed (Asymmetric) Graphs

`asymmetric_popgraph()` produces a directed graph where each undirected edge becomes two directed edges with weights reflecting the net introgression pressure. `geom_edge_fan()` automatically curves parallel edges so both directions are visible.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
lopho_asym <- lopho_dec |>
  asymmetric_popgraph()

lopho_asym |>
  ggraph( layout = "manual",
          x = igraph::V( lopho_asym )$Longitude,
          y = igraph::V( lopho_asym )$Latitude ) +
  geom_sf( data = land,
           fill = "grey92",
           colour = "grey55",
           linewidth = 0.3 ) +
  geom_edge_fan( aes( color = weight, width = weight ),
                 arrow = arrow( length = unit( 2.5, "mm" ),
                                type = "closed" ),
                 end_cap = circle( 3, "mm" ),
                 show.legend = FALSE ) +
  scale_edge_width( range = c( 0.3, 2 ), guide = "none" ) +
  scale_edge_color_viridis( option = "magma",
                            alpha = 0.4,
                            guide = "none" ) +
  geom_node_point( size = 3, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 0.8 ) +
  coord_sf( xlim = c( -116, -108.5 ),
            ylim = c( 22.5, 32.5 ) ) +
  labs( title = "Asymmetric Gene Flow — Lophocereus",
        x = NULL,
        y = NULL ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Interactive Leaflet Maps

`addAlleleFrequencies()` adds allele-frequency pie charts to a leaflet map and follows the standard leaflet pipe pattern. Pre-compute frequencies with `frequencies()`, build the base map from `strata_coordinates()`, then pipe into `addAlleleFrequencies()`.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library( leaflet )
library( leaflet.minicharts )

freqs <- arapat |>
  frequencies( loci = "LTRS", stratum = "Species" )

arapat |>
  strata_coordinates( stratum = "Species" ) |>
  leaflet() |>
  addTiles() |>
  addAlleleFrequencies( freqs )
```

Pass `locus =` explicitly when `freqs` contains more than one locus. Width and height of the pie charts (in pixels) are controlled with `width =` and `height =`.

## Without Pipes

```{r}
#| eval: false
freqs <- frequencies( arapat, loci = "LTRS", stratum = "Species" )
ggplot( freqs, aes( x = Allele, y = Frequency, fill = Stratum ) ) +
  geom_col( position = "dodge" )

coords <- strata_coordinates( arapat )
baja_map +
  geom_point( aes( x = Longitude, y = Latitude ), data = coords )
plot( lopho_dec, base = baja_map )

lopho_dec <- decorate_graph( lopho, baja, stratum = "Population" )
ggraph( lopho_dec,
        layout = "manual",
        x = igraph::V( lopho_dec )$Longitude,
        y = igraph::V( lopho_dec )$Latitude ) +
  geom_sf( data = land, fill = "grey92", colour = "grey55" ) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point() +
  coord_sf()
```
